items.caption: Figure 1: (left) Transformer architecture and training objectives used in this work. (right) Input transformations for fine-tuning on different tasks. We convert all structured inputs into token sequences to be processed by our pre-trained model, followed by a linear+softmax layer.
items.title: One Stack, Four Input Shapes
items.takeaway: The figure shows that a single decoder-only transformer, pre-trained once, serves every task in the paper: the left panel draws the block that is repeated twelve times and the two heads that sit on it, and the right panel shows that adapting to a new task means rewriting its input as one token sequence rather than redesigning the network. The only task-specific machinery is the added linear layer and the special tokens marking where the parts of an input begin and end.
items.walkthrough:
Two diagrams sit side by side. The left one is the network and its training objectives. The right one is how four different kinds of task input are rewritten so that same network can read them.

### Reading the left panel

Start at the bottom. **Text & Position Embed** is the layer-zero input [[input-representation-h0]]: each token's embedding added to a vector for its slot in the sequence, where those slot vectors are trained rather than fixed sinusoids [[learned-position-embeddings]].

The arrow goes up into the blue box. Inside, **Masked Multi Self Attention** [[masked-self-attention]] lets each position attend to itself and earlier positions only, never later ones. The circled plus is the residual add, and **Layer Norm** [[layer-normalization-gpt1]] follows it. Then **Feed Forward** [[position-wise-feedforward-3072]], another add, another norm.

The **12x** bracket on the far left says this whole block is stacked twelve times [[twelve-layer-depth]], one feeding the next. That stack is the [[multi-layer-transformer-decoder]] — a [[decoder-only-stack]], with no encoder half.

Two arrows leave the top into two heads. **Text Prediction** is the next-token objective used for pre-training [[language-modeling-objective]] and kept during fine-tuning as an auxiliary term [[auxiliary-lm-objective]]. **Task Classifier** is the added output layer [[linear-output-layer-wy]]. Both draw on the same stack.

### Reading the right panel

Each row is one task family. The coloured boxes left of the bracket are a token sequence built by walking a structured input into one ordered line [[traversal-style-approach]]. **Start** and **Extract** are the randomly initialized bracketing tokens [[start-and-end-tokens]]; **Delim** is a `$` marking where one part ends [[delimiter-token]]. Extract is named for its job: its final-layer activation is what the classifier reads [[final-token-activation]].

Classification is one span. Entailment concatenates premise and hypothesis [[entailment-input-transformation]].

Similarity draws **two** rows because the pair has no natural order [[similarity-input-transformation]]. Both orderings are run separately, and the circled plus adds the two representations element-wise before one **Linear** layer sees them.

Multiple Choice builds one row per candidate answer [[qa-and-commonsense-input-transformation]]. Each row gets its own Linear head producing one score, and the small bar box on the right is the softmax over those scores.

Nothing in the blue stack changes across rows — that is the claim of a [[task-agnostic-model]].

terms.definition: The orange box at the bottom of the left panel: the input to layer zero, formed by adding each token's embedding to a learned vector for its position in the sequence. The paper writes this as $h_0 = UW_e + W_p$.
The pink box: multi-head self-attention restricted so each position may attend only to itself and to earlier positions. The mask is what makes the stack usable as a left-to-right language model.
The residual add: the sublayer's output is summed with the input that entered it, before normalization. Two appear per block, one after attention and one after the feed-forward.
The purple boxes: per-position normalization of activations to zero mean and unit variance with a learned gain and bias. It appears twice per block, after each residual add.
The yellow box: the position-wise feed-forward sublayer, applied to each position independently. In the trained model it expands 768 dimensions to 3072 and projects back down, with GELU in between.
The bracket label on the far left of the blue box: the whole block drawn inside it is repeated twelve times, each layer's output feeding the next. It is not twelve parallel copies.
The repeated unit of the stack: masked self-attention, residual add, layer norm, feed-forward, residual add, layer norm. Drawn once and multiplied by the 12x bracket.
The green head on the left: the next-token language modelling objective $L_1$. It is the only objective during pre-training, and stays on as a weighted auxiliary term during fine-tuning.

The green head on the right: the supervised objective $L_2$, computed from a linear layer over the final activation. Both heads are drawn on the same stack because the paper trains them together during fine-tuning.
The first row on the right: a task whose input is a single span of text, such as sentiment or grammatical acceptability. It needs no restructuring beyond the bracketing tokens.
The second row: given a premise and a hypothesis, decide whether the premise entails it, contradicts it, or leaves it open. The two parts are concatenated with a delimiter between them.
The third row: decide whether two sentences mean the same thing. Because neither sentence is naturally first, both orderings are built and processed.
The fourth row: reading comprehension and commonsense tasks, where a context and question come with several candidate answers. One sequence is built per candidate.
The randomly initialized start token, written $\langle s\rangle$ in the text, placed at the front of every transformed sequence. Its embedding is one of the few parameters added at fine-tuning time.
The delimiter token, written `$` in the text, inserted between the parts of a structured input to mark where one part ends and the next begins.
The end token $\langle e\rangle$ closing every sequence. It is labelled Extract because the final block's activation at this last position is the vector handed to the linear classifier.
The single input span in the Classification row: the sentence or document being labelled.
In the Entailment row, the statement assumed true. It is placed first in the sequence.
In the Entailment row, the statement whose status relative to the premise is being judged. It follows the delimiter.
The two sentences of a similarity pair. They appear in both orders across the two rows, so the model never sees only one arrangement.
In the Multiple Choice row, the document and question concatenated together, written $[z; q]$ in the text. It is repeated identically in every row of that block.
The candidate answers, one per row. Each is appended after the delimiter to the same context.
A stand-in for the entire twelve-layer stack drawn in the left panel. Every green box in the right panel is the same pre-trained weights, not a separate model.
The added output layer $W_y$ mapping the extracted activation to label scores, followed by a softmax. It is one of only two things added per task, the other being delimiter embeddings.
Element-wise addition of the two sequence representations produced by the two orderings, before the single linear layer. Adding makes the result the same whichever sentence was called first.

terms.term: Bar box (right of the Multiple Choice Linear heads)
terms.definition: The small box with bars of different lengths: the output distribution over candidate answers, obtained by softmaxing the per-answer scores against each other.

terms.term: Bracket (between the token row and the Transformer box)
terms.definition: The tall brace on each row, grouping the token sequence as the single input handed to the stack. It carries no computation of its own.

numbers.meaning: The number of times the drawn transformer block is stacked. The paper's model specification states a 12-layer decoder-only transformer; the analysis section then treats that depth as a dial, transferring varying numbers of these layers into fine-tuning.

Two rows because a similarity pair has no inherent ordering. The paper builds both orderings, processes each independently, and adds the results, so the prediction does not depend on which sentence was placed first.
One row per candidate answer, with N standing for however many the dataset provides. RACE questions come with four options and the Story Cloze Test with two, so the figure leaves the count open.
Three rows are drawn only to show the pattern — first, second, and Nth. The vertical spacing implies the omitted middle rows.
The width of every token representation at every layer, from the embedding box to the top of the stack. Named in the model specification, not printed in the figure.

The Masked Multi Self Attention box splits into twelve parallel heads, each attending in a 64-dimensional subspace since 768 divided by 12 is 64. Coincidentally equal to the layer count, but a separate setting.
The inner width of the Feed Forward box: 768 in, 3072 in the middle, 768 out. Four times the state size, following the original transformer.

The weight on the Text Prediction head during fine-tuning, in $L_3 = L_2 + \lambda L_1$. At 0.5 the language modelling term counts half as much as the task loss; the paper reports it helped generalization and convergence.
The context window in tokens, so the widest input any row of the right panel can present to the stack. Pre-training used contiguous sequences of this length.

items.caption: Table 1: A list of the different tasks and datasets used in our experiments.
items.title: The Twelve Evaluation Datasets
items.takeaway: This table is the paper's full evaluation menu: four families of supervised language understanding tasks covering twelve datasets in total. It establishes the breadth the paper is claiming for one pre-trained model, since the same weights are fine-tuned for every row rather than a different architecture being built per task.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at a two-column list, not a results table. The left column, "Task", names a family of supervised problems. The right column, "Datasets", names the specific benchmarks the paper fine-tunes and evaluates on inside that family. The bracketed numbers are citations to the papers that released each dataset, nothing more. Read it as an inventory: four rows, twelve datasets, and this is the complete set behind every number reported later. The paper calls this the [[evaluation-task-families]] set, and draws several entries from the [[glue-benchmark]], a then-recent bundle of language understanding datasets.

Row one is [[natural-language-inference]]: read a premise and a hypothesis, then judge whether the premise entails it, contradicts it, or leaves it undecided. Five datasets stress that same task over different source text. [[snli]] is built from image captions. [[multinli]] mixes transcribed speech, popular fiction and government reports. [[qnli]] comes from Wikipedia articles. [[scitail]] is derived from science exam questions. [[rte]] is drawn from news.

Row two is question answering, which the paper pairs with commonsense reasoning. [[race-dataset]] gives English exam passages from middle and high school with multiple-choice questions attached; the paper picks it because it says the questions demand more reasoning than other reading comprehension sets. [[story-cloze-test]] gives a short multi-sentence story and two candidate endings, and asks which one actually finishes it.

Row three is sentence similarity, also called paraphrase detection: decide whether two sentences mean the same thing. [[mrpc]] pairs sentences from news sources. [[qqp]] pairs Quora questions and asks whether they ask the same thing. [[sts-b]] scores sentence pairs for degree of similarity.

Row four is [[text-classification]], where the input is a single sentence. [[sst-2]] asks for binary sentiment. [[cola]] asks whether a sentence is grammatically acceptable, judged by experts.

Notice the structural variety across rows: sentence pairs, document-question-answer triplets, single sentences. Handling all of it with one unchanged network is exactly what the [[task-specific-input-transformations]] are for, and what the paper means by a [[task-agnostic-model]]. Against these twelve, it reports [[state-of-the-art-9-of-12]].

terms.definition: The left column header. Each entry under it names a family of supervised problems that share a common input shape and a common notion of a correct answer.
The right column header. Each entry under it is a specific labelled benchmark the paper fine-tunes on and reports a score for.

The first task family: given a premise sentence and a hypothesis sentence, decide whether the premise entails the hypothesis, contradicts it, or is neutral toward it. Also called recognizing textual entailment.
Stanford Natural Language Inference. An NLI dataset whose premises come from image captions; the paper describes it as the largest dataset in the whole evaluation.
A multi-genre NLI dataset, spanning transcribed speech, popular fiction and government reports, so a model cannot rely on one text style. Also written MNLI in the results tables.

QNLI, an NLI dataset built over Wikipedia articles in which a question and a sentence are paired and the model decides whether the sentence answers the question. The paper reports its largest NLI gain here.
Recognizing Textual Entailment, an NLI dataset over news articles from the PASCAL challenge series. It is small, and it is the one NLI dataset where the paper does not beat the previous best.
An entailment dataset constructed from science exam questions, so the premises and hypotheses carry science-domain content rather than everyday description.
The second task family, which the paper elsewhere widens to question answering and commonsense reasoning. It asks the model to reason across one or several sentences of a passage to select an answer.

A reading comprehension dataset of English passages and multiple-choice questions taken from Chinese middle and high school exams. The paper chooses it on the grounds that it contains more reasoning-type questions than earlier comprehension sets.
The Story Cloze Test: given a multi-sentence story, pick which of two candidate final sentences is the correct ending. It tests commonsense expectations about how situations resolve.
The third task family, also called paraphrase detection: decide whether two sentences are semantically equivalent, which requires handling rephrasing, negation and syntactic ambiguity.
MRPC, a paraphrase detection dataset of sentence pairs collected from news sources and labelled for whether each pair says the same thing.
QQP, a dataset of pairs of questions posted to Quora, each labelled for whether the two questions are asking the same thing.

STS-B, the Semantic Textual Similarity benchmark from a SemEval shared task, where sentence pairs carry a graded similarity score rather than a binary same/different label. It is the smallest training set in the evaluation.
The fourth task family. Here the input is a single sentence with no second part, and the model assigns it one label.
SST-2, the two-class version of the Stanford Sentiment Treebank: label a sentence as positive or negative sentiment.
The Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability: expert judgements on whether a sentence is grammatical. The paper uses it as a probe of what it calls a model's innate linguistic bias.
Reference markers pointing into the paper's bibliography, identifying the work that released each dataset. They carry no experimental meaning.

numbers.meaning: The number of rows, and so the number of task families the paper groups its evaluation into: natural language inference, question answering, sentence similarity, and classification. Section 4.2 lists the same four.
The total dataset count across the four rows: 5 + 2 + 3 + 2. The paper's headline claim is stated against this denominator.
Datasets in the natural language inference row (SNLI, MultiNLI, Question NLI, RTE, SciTail). The paper says it beats the previous best on four of these five, RTE being the exception.
Datasets in the question answering row: RACE and Story Cloze. It is the shortest row, but the paper leans on it for the claim about handling long-range context.
Datasets in the sentence similarity row (MRPC, QQP, STS Benchmark). The paper reports state-of-the-art results on two of these three.
Datasets in the classification row: SST-2 and CoLA. Both take a single sentence as input rather than a pair.
Not a citation. It marks the two-class variant of the Sentiment Treebank, positive versus negative, as opposed to the finer-grained five-way version of the same corpus.
Cites Bowman et al., 2015, the paper that released SNLI.
Cites Williams et al., 2018, the paper that released MultiNLI.
Cites Wang et al., 2018, the GLUE benchmark paper. Question NLI is attributed to GLUE because it is packaged and distributed there rather than as a standalone release.
Cites Bentivogli et al., 2009, the fifth PASCAL recognizing textual entailment challenge, the source of RTE.
Cites Khot et al., 2018, the paper that released SciTail.
Cites Lai et al., 2017, the paper that released RACE.
Cites Mostafazadeh et al., 2017, the LSDSem shared task paper defining the Story Cloze Test.
Cites Dolan and Brockett, 2005, the paper that released the MSR Paraphrase Corpus.
Cites Chen et al., 2018, the Quora data release for the Question Pairs dataset.
Cites Cer et al., 2017, the SemEval-2017 Task 1 paper behind the STS Benchmark.
Cites Socher et al., 2013, the paper that released the Stanford Sentiment Treebank.
Cites Warstadt et al., 2018, the CoLA release.
Not printed in the table, but the count it underwrites: Section 4.2 reports new state-of-the-art results on nine of these twelve datasets, in many cases against ensembles.
Training-example counts the paper gives for the largest and smallest datasets in this list, SNLI and STS-B respectively, used to argue the method works across dataset sizes.
Training examples in RTE, the figure the paper offers to explain why it underperforms there (56% accuracy against a prior 61.7%).

items.caption: Table 2: Experimental results on natural language inference tasks, comparing our model with current state-of-the-art methods. 5x indicates an ensemble of 5 models. All datasets use accuracy as the evaluation metric.
items.title: NLI Benchmark Scoreboard
items.takeaway: Table 2 compares one fine-tuned general model against task-built baselines on five natural language inference datasets, and reports it ahead on four of them — by 1.5 points on MNLI, 5 on SciTail, 5.8 on QNLI and 0.6 on SNLI — while losing on RTE, the smallest dataset, where a multi-task biLSTM scores 61.7 against this model's 56.0.
items.walkthrough:
Table 2 is the scoreboard for one of the four task families in the paper's evaluation: [[natural-language-inference]]. The task is to read a premise and a hypothesis and judge the relationship between them as entailment, contradiction, or neutral. Rows are systems; columns are the five datasets those systems are measured on.

Every cell is accuracy in percent. The caption says all datasets here use accuracy, so numbers are comparable down a column. They are not comparable across columns, since each dataset has its own difficulty and its own label set.

A dash means that system reported no number there. Most baselines are built for one or two datasets, so most of the grid is empty.

### The columns

[[multinli]] is split in two. MNLI-m is the matched development set, whose text genres also appear in training; MNLI-mm is the mismatched set, drawn from genres held out. [[snli]] is the largest dataset in the whole evaluation, roughly 550k training pairs from image captions. [[scitail]] comes from science exams, [[qnli]] from Wikipedia, and [[rte]] from news articles with only 2,490 training examples.

### The row blocks

Three horizontal rules cut the rows into four blocks. The top block is ensembles: `5x` means five separately trained copies whose predictions are combined, `3x` means three. The second block is CAFE again as a single model, which is why every score sits a point or so below its own `5x` row. The third block is two multi-task baselines from the [[glue-benchmark]] paper, each trained on many tasks at once — which is why they, alone among the [[baseline-comparisons]], can fill the QNLI and RTE columns. The bottom block is this paper's model: one [[task-agnostic-model]], fine-tuned per task, not an ensemble.

Bold marks the best number in a column. Underline marks the best prior result in columns where the bold belongs to this paper.

### What it shows

Take MNLI-m: the underlined 80.6 is the ensemble Stochastic Answer Network, and 82.1 beats it by 1.5 points. The same subtraction gives 5.0 on SciTail, 5.8 on QNLI, and 0.6 on SNLI — the [[absolute-improvement]] figures quoted in the text.

RTE is the exception. At 56.0 the model falls 5.7 points short of 61.7. The paper attributes this to RTE's size and suggests multi-task training would likely help, while noting it did not try that.

terms.definition: The first column, listing the systems being compared. Each row is one system, identified by name, citation number, and ensemble size if it is an ensemble.
The matched development set of MultiNLI, where the test text comes from the same genres seen during training. Higher accuracy is better.

The mismatched development set of MultiNLI, drawn from genres held out of training, so it measures how well a system transfers across text genres. It is the harder of the two MNLI columns for almost every row here.
The Stanford Natural Language Inference dataset, built from image captions and the largest dataset in the paper's whole evaluation at roughly 550k training pairs.
An entailment dataset constructed from science exam questions. It is the column where the paper reports its largest absolute gain alongside QNLI.
A natural language inference dataset built over Wikipedia articles, part of the GLUE bundle. Only the multi-task baselines and this paper's model report numbers in this column.
Recognizing Textual Entailment, a small NLI dataset over news articles with 2,490 training examples. It is the one column here where this paper's model does not win.
An Enhanced Sequential Inference Model — a task-specific biLSTM architecture for NLI — with ELMo representations added as input features, run as a five-model ensemble. It reports only an SNLI number.

Deep contextualized word representations from a pre-trained bidirectional language model, fed into a separate task model as extra features rather than fine-tuned. It is the feature-based transfer approach this paper contrasts itself with.
A compare-propagate architecture with alignment factorization, a task-specific NLI model of Tay et al. It appears twice in the table, once as a five-model ensemble and once as a single model.
An NLI model of Liu et al. that makes its prediction through multiple stochastic inference steps, run here as a three-model ensemble. It holds the previous best on both MNLI columns.
A multi-task sentence representation baseline reported in the GLUE paper. Because it is trained across tasks, it can report QNLI and RTE numbers that the single-dataset NLI systems cannot.
A bidirectional LSTM with attention trained on multiple GLUE tasks at once. It is the system that beats this paper's model on RTE.
This paper's system: the transformer language model pre-trained on BooksCorpus, then fine-tuned on each dataset with the entailment input transformation. It is a single model, not an ensemble.
Marks a row as an ensemble of five separately trained models whose predictions are combined. The caption defines it explicitly.
The same convention for an ensemble of three models. It appears only on the Stochastic Answer Network row.
The evaluation metric for every cell: the fraction of pairs whose relationship label the system predicts correctly, expressed as a percentage.
A cell where that system reports no result for that dataset, usually because it was never evaluated on it. It is not a score of zero and should not be read as a failure.
Marks the highest accuracy in a column. It falls on this paper's model in five of six columns and on Multi-task BiLSTM + Attn in the RTE column.

Marks the best previous published result in a column, in the columns where the bold has gone to this paper's model. The gap between an underline and the bold below it is the paper's claimed absolute improvement.

The three interior rules group rows into ensembles, single-model task-specific systems, multi-task GLUE baselines, and this paper's model. They mark what kind of comparison each block is, not a ranking.
Bracketed citation numbers into the paper's reference list: [44] Peters et al. (ELMo), [58] Tay et al. (CAFE), [35] Liu et al. (Stochastic Answer Network), [64] Wang et al. (GLUE benchmark).
Also called recognizing textual entailment: read a premise and a hypothesis, then choose entailment, contradiction, or neutral. All six columns are instances of this task.
Training one model on several labelled tasks simultaneously, which is what the two [64] baselines do. The paper suggests this is why they hold up on the tiny RTE dataset.
The caption's term for the baseline rows: the best published systems on each dataset at the time of writing, most of them architectures designed for NLI specifically.

The same ensemble on mismatched MNLI, 1.2 points below its own matched score — the usual pattern, since mismatched genres are unseen in training.
CAFE's ensemble ties ESIM+ELMo's ensemble exactly on SNLI. Both are underlined as joint previous best.
The previous best on matched MNLI, from a three-model ensemble, hence underlined. This paper's 1.5-point MNLI claim is measured against it.
The previous best on mismatched MNLI. This paper's 81.4 exceeds it by 1.3 points.
Single-model CAFE on matched MNLI, 1.5 points below its own 5x ensemble row. The gap is the price of dropping the ensemble.
Single-model CAFE on mismatched MNLI, 1.1 points below its 5x version.
Single-model CAFE on SNLI, 0.8 below its ensemble's 89.3 and 1.4 below this paper's 89.9.
The only reported SciTail baseline in the table, and therefore the underlined previous best. This paper's 88.3 is 5.0 points above it.
GenSen's MNLI scores, roughly nine points below the dedicated NLI systems. A multi-task sentence encoder gives up accuracy on any one task in exchange for covering many.
The best baseline QNLI number, hence underlined. This paper's 88.1 clears it by 5.8 points, its largest NLI gain.
GenSen's RTE accuracy. It is above this paper's 56.0 but below the 61.7 that takes the bold.
This baseline's MNLI scores, slightly ahead of GenSen but roughly ten points behind this paper's model.
Its QNLI accuracy, 0.2 below GenSen's underlined 82.3. Note this cell shares its value with the paper's MNLI-m result — the same digits in a different column.
The only bold number not on the paper's own row. It is the best RTE result in the table and beats this paper's model by 5.7 points.
This paper's matched MNLI accuracy: 80.6 + 1.5, the source of the abstract's 1.5% textual entailment claim.
Mismatched MNLI, 1.3 points over the previous best 80.1. The model loses only 0.7 points moving from matched to mismatched genres.
SNLI accuracy, 0.6 above the two underlined 89.3 ensembles. The smallest of the paper's four NLI wins, on the largest dataset.

QNLI accuracy, 5.8 points above GenSen's 82.3.
The paper's RTE accuracy and its one loss in this table — below both [64] baselines. The text attributes it to RTE's small training set.
The number of separately trained models combined in an ensemble row. The paper notes its single model still beats several of these ensembles.
RTE's training set size, quoted in the text as the reason for the loss: too few labelled examples for fine-tuning alone to carry the model.
SNLI's approximate training set size, quoted elsewhere in the paper as the largest of the twelve datasets. It sits at the opposite end of the size range from RTE.
The four absolute improvements the text quotes, on MNLI, SciTail, QNLI and SNLI. Each is a bold cell minus the underlined cell above it in the same column.
The RTE shortfall: 61.7 minus 56.0. The paper states the loss rather than the difference, but this is its size.
How many of the five NLI datasets the paper claims to win, counting MNLI-m and MNLI-mm as one dataset. RTE is the fifth.

items.caption: Table 3: Results on question answering and commonsense reasoning, comparing our model with current state-of-the-art methods.. 9x means an ensemble of 9 models.
items.title: RACE and Story Cloze Results
items.takeaway: On the paper's two reading-and-reasoning benchmarks, a single fine-tuned transformer language model beats every previously published system, by 8.9 accuracy points on the Story Cloze Test and 5.7 points on RACE overall. The RACE baselines it passes are 9-model ensembles, while the paper's entry is one model.
items.walkthrough:
This is the results table for the paper's [[question-answering-and-commonsense-reasoning]] family: two datasets, four score columns, five systems.

Each row is a system and each column is a test set. Higher is better, and every number is an accuracy percentage. A dash means that system never reported a result on that dataset, so the row is simply blank there rather than scoring zero. The underlined number in each column is the best previously published result; the bold bottom row is this paper's model.

The datasets. [[story-cloze-test]] gives a multi-sentence story and two candidate endings, and asks which one is correct. [[race-dataset]] is reading comprehension built from English middle-school and high-school exam passages. RACE-m is the middle-school split, RACE-h the high-school split, and RACE the combined figure. Note that the combined score is not the average of the two splits: for the paper's model, 62.9 and 57.4 combine to 59.0, which sits nearer the high-school number, consistent with the high-school portion contributing more test questions. The same pattern holds for the baseline rows.

The "(9x)" annotation. Both RACE baselines are ensembles of nine separately trained models whose predictions are pooled — a standard way to buy a point or two of accuracy at nine times the compute. The paper's row carries no such annotation. It is one model, fine-tuned once per dataset from the same pre-trained weights ([[supervised-fine-tuning]]), with each candidate answer scored by appending it to the passage and question ([[qa-and-commonsense-input-transformation]]).

The margins. On Story Cloze, $86.5 - 77.6 = 8.9$. On RACE overall, $59.0 - 53.3 = 5.7$. Both are the [[absolute-improvement]] figures quoted in Section 4.2. The split columns show the gap is uneven: RACE-m improves by $62.9 - 60.2 = 2.7$, while RACE-h improves by $57.4 - 50.3 = 7.1$, so most of the RACE gain comes from the harder high-school questions.

The paper reads these margins as evidence that pre-training on long stretches of contiguous text lets the model use [[long-range-dependencies-gpt1]] — the passage detail several sentences away that answers the question. That is an interpretation, not something the table measures directly.

terms.definition: The first column, listing the system being scored. Four prior published systems on top, the paper's own model on the bottom row.
Column for the Story Cloze Test: given a multi-sentence story, pick the correct ending out of two candidates. Scores are accuracy, so 50 would be chance.
The middle-school split of RACE — exam reading-comprehension questions written for younger students, and the easier of the two splits for every system in the table.
The high-school split of RACE. Every system scores lower here than on RACE-m, which is where the paper's largest RACE gain comes from.

The combined score over both RACE splits. It is not the plain average of RACE-m and RACE-h; it lands closer to RACE-h, consistent with the high-school portion being the larger share of the test questions.
A prior Story Cloze system (Srinivasan, Arora and Riedl, 2018), cited in the paper as reference 55. Included as a Story Cloze baseline only; it reports nothing on RACE.
A prior Story Cloze system (Chaturvedi, Peng and Roth, 2017), reference 7. Its 77.6 is the underlined previous best on Story Cloze.
A prior RACE system (Xu et al., 2017), reference 67, evaluated as a 9-model ensemble. It reports no Story Cloze result.
A prior RACE system (Tay, Tuan and Hui, 2018), reference 59, also a 9-model ensemble. It holds the underlined previous best in all three RACE columns.
The caption's shorthand: this row is an ensemble of 9 separately trained models whose predictions are pooled. It marks the baseline as costing roughly nine times the compute of a single model.
The paper's own system: the pre-trained decoder-only transformer language model, fine-tuned on each task's labelled data. One model per task, not an ensemble.
Typographic marker for the paper's own results. Here bold also happens to mark the best score in every column.
Marks the best previously published result in each column — the number the paper's margin is measured against.
No result reported by that system on that dataset. It signals a missing entry, not a score of zero, so those cells carry no information about the system's ability.
